briefing.text: "I'm told there's a roll of paper in this valley I'd rather not read," Reed says. "I haven't asked to." She signs something without looking up. "If it becomes evidence, bring it to me before anyone else."
"There was smoke on the Row. I didn't go and look," Reed says. "Someone will ask what I saw. I'll say I was at my desk, because I was."

"Word's gone round that there's a retainer paper out on you," Reed says evenly. "It's lawful, so I can't touch it. When they first ask something of you, I'd like to know which side of the desk you're sitting on."
"Forty-one names," Reed says, tapping a page she hasn't turned since. "No law broken, nobody to charge. I wrote it all down anyway. It'll be there when someone wants it. Someone will."
Reed stays seated. "I have eleven men and a town without a granary. If you've come for work, there's none. If you want me to tell you it wasn't your fault, I can't do that either."
"East gate shuts at dusk now. Nobody argued." She signs a chit without reading it. "Seems emptying the quarry once was enough to stop the council having opinions about it."

choices.label: That's a lot of authority for one road.

briefing.text: "Two of my watchmen resigned this week. One spat on my boots as he left." Reed sounds almost cheerful. "The quarry sent eleven tons of dressed stone for the bridge, free of charge. Ask me in a year."

Reed listens to the whole story standing at the well in the middle of the market. She does not interrupt.

"Fourteen quarters," she says when you finish. "A house account at Greyhythe. Four days before each payment, always exactly what was short."

She looks across the square at two of her men leaning by the well.

"I signed for that money twelve times with my own hand," says Captain Elowen Reed. "So whatever this is, I'm in the middle of it, and I have been for over a year. They didn't have to buy me. They only had to let me think the roll was met."

choices.label: Send it back. Make the council find it.
Say nothing. A watch of twenty-six beats a watch of eighteen.
Your men should hear it from you, not from a rumour.

briefing.text: "Ashe," Reed says. "Second desk, counting house. In six years, he's never volunteered anything, and he's never refused to answer. I only recently realised those are the same policy."

"Twenty-two men," Reed says. "No night patrol west of the High Street. Every coin I pay them comes from a vote I sat through." She rubs her eyes, something you haven't seen her do. "Ask me in a year if four men were worth it. I'll have an answer by then. I don't now."

Quarter day comes. The money is there, and Reed signs for it without looking up. That is all.

"Twenty-six men, paid on the day," she says afterwards. "I wrote it down in my own book. Not the day book. Mine." She caps the ink. "So there's one honest account of this in Rivermark, in a drawer in my own house. I know that isn't the same as honesty."

choices.label: You did the arithmetic anyone would have done.

briefing.text: "Six of them have stopped calling me Captain when I'm out of the room," Reed says. "Ballow said it: 'Then who is it we work for, and how would we know?' Every man in the guardroom has been carrying that question since." She squares her shoulders. "They kept the money. I would have too. That isn't what will do the damage."
Reed looks past you at Aldric, who has been in her doorway for some time. "Brother. You look like you're about to complicate my afternoon."

choices.label: He has something to say. Let him say it.
He's here about the raids. Nothing else.

briefing.text: "You're going east, then." She turns the muster roll face down. "I won't tell you what to do down there. If I give the order and it goes wrong, it's mine. Do you see how that works?"

choices.label: You want it done and you want it deniable.
What do you actually know about the warren?

briefing.text: "The road is quiet," Reed says, "and I can't pretend that settles it anymore." She turns the map toward you. "There's a hole in that hill with a warlord in it, and a town that's argued about it for eleven years. I'd like it settled while I still have eleven men."

choices.label: Then I'll go east and settle it.

briefing.text: "Go on," Reed says before you speak. "You look like someone who's counted something twice."

choices.label: Every wagon they hit was carrying granary grain.

briefing.text: "The road, then. Four caravans, all within two miles of the quarry cut." She taps the map twice in the same place. "I've walked it. There's nothing special about that stretch, except that it's where they always strike."
Reed's eyes move from your face to the book under your arm. "That's the mill ledger. The actual mill ledger, here in this room, on a Tuesday."

choices.label: First you tell me what happens to Sera Vance.

briefing.text: "Still looking? Good. No one else in this town will."

choices.label: There's a man at the granary you should be looking at.

briefing.text: "The mill business is closed," Reed says, in a tone that ends the matter. "There's still a road east of here."

choices.label: You have been holding a piece of paper this whole conversation.

briefing.text: "You'll be the ones off the west road." Reed stays seated. "I have two problems. One's quiet enough that I'd rather ask about it quietly."

choices.label: You have been holding a piece of paper this whole conversation.

the_ledger_offer.text: "The mill accounts don't add up. Six caravans paid for grain that was never carted, over two years, all in the same neat hand." She slides over a scrap of paper. "I want to know whose hand before I bring this to the watch."

her_own_men.text: "Three of my eleven have wives working in the granary loft," Reed says. "Another has a brother who carts for them. I can ask my own men whatever I like; I'll get eleven versions of the same shrug."

the_ledger.text: "Sera Vance. She's kept the books since her father died, and she keeps them alone. That's bothered me for a year."

interjections.text: Kessa: "One clerk, two years, and nobody looked. That's not a thief. That's a town that didn't want to know."

choices.label: You already know it's not her idea.

she_admits_it.text: Reed is quiet a moment. "A mill clerk doesn't benefit from grain that never moves. Someone who buys grain does." She taps the desk. "I can arrest a clerk. Bring me the book, and I'll have a reason to look at anyone else."

she_wont_say.text: "No," Reed says. "I have a rank, eleven men and no evidence. Say a name in this room, and it becomes a rumour with a captain's seal. Bring me something in writing."

what_happens_to_sera.text: Reed doesn't lie. "Her name is on every false entry, and nobody else's. She'll be held and tried at the spring assize. She'll be found to have done it, because she did." She pauses. "If you want a different answer, bring me a different book."

she_takes_it.text: Reed takes the book silently and locks it in her desk. She turns the key twice, then rests a hand on the lid. That is the part she'll remember.

interjections.text: Sera looks at the desk, not at either of you.
Aldric, quietly: "That was right. You're allowed to feel how you feel."
Kessa snorts. "That was easier than it should've been."

name_marrow.text: "Marrow." Reed says the name flatly, as if she's been holding it back. "Yes. I know. I've known for eleven months and haven't been able to act on it."

choices.label: Then let me push him where you can't.
Bring the ledger and it's over.

name_marrow.text: You put the stamped tally on her desk. Reed turns it over. "Eighteen sacks, granary mark, and Mara Hearthstone never ordered them." She sets it down. "That's a stick. Bring me a book."
"Which man? And where is it written down?" Reed waits a moment. "I'm not being difficult. That's my whole job."

she_gives_you_room.text: "All right." Reed sits back. "You're not the watch, and I haven't instructed you. If you stand on the weighing floor and make yourself a nuisance, no report will reach my desk for at least a day."

she_puts_a_watch_on_you.text: "No." Reed stands. "You're asking me to authorise someone with a sword to lean on a taxpayer. Corwin, go with them. Stay with them." A watchman steps away from the wall. "He's not there to protect you."

interjections.text: Sera, under her breath: "Brilliant. Now we do everything with an audience."

the_raids.text: "Four caravans in six weeks. Goblins from the eastern hills, with gnolls among them. That's new, and I don't like it." She smooths the map. "Make the road safe. I don't much mind how."

the_warden_hint.text: Reed looks at Ilse for a moment. "You have her. Right." She puts the pin back in the map without marking it. "Thornwood has counted every goblin on that hill for two years, and this office never asked her for the number. I'd like that on the record as something I inherited." She turns to you. "You don't need an introduction. Ask her about the ground between the cut and the second ford, then bring me what she says."

interjections.text: Ilse, evenly, looking at the map instead of Reed: "Eleven in spring, thirty by midsummer, forty-one the week the wagons started going over. The number's been available."

the_warden_hint.text: "Ilse Thornwood. A warden, of sorts. The post is older than the town, and nobody's got round to abolishing it." Reed shrugs. "She's counted every goblin on that hill for two years. No one's asked her."

choices.label: She is at my camp. I will ask her.

the_pattern_report.text: Reed listens without moving. Then she says, "Six weeks. Four wagons. All contracted to the granary, and nothing else." She plants both hands on the desk. "Go on."

interjections.text: Ilse: "They were told which wagon. Twice they let one pass and went back up the slope. Goblins don't do that when they're hungry."
Kessa: "Someone's paying them. That's no raid. It's a contract."
Sera has gone pale.

choices.label: Somebody in Rivermark is paying them to hit those wagons.
That's as far as I've got.

she_believes_you.text: "I suspected it after the second one," Reed says. "I said nothing. The alternative was accusing in council the man who lends them money." She looks tired for a moment. "See it through. However you can."

the_warren.text: "Old winding shaft, east side of the cut. It goes deeper than anyone alive has been." Reed's finger stops on the map. "They came up four years ago, all in one week. Not a trickle. The whole tribe, in midwinter, into the worst ground on the hill."

interjections.text: Ilse: "No tribe walks into winter for no reason. I've been telling that to a shed for two years."
Aldric: "In one week. In winter. Something drove them out."

choices.label: I want that in writing before I go.

she_writes_it.text: Reed writes four lines, seals them and hands you the paper. "It says you act under the watch's authority east of the gate. It's worth exactly as much as I am, which this month isn't nothing."

no_writ.text: "No." Reed sets down the pen. "If I sign, everything you do out there is mine. Go east on your own, as a private person. If it goes badly, I can keep my post and go on serving the town."

deniable.text: "It is," Reed agrees. "I have eleven men, a council that owes money to the wrong person, and one road. I keep this town with what little I have. You're the most expendable useful person who's walked through that door in two years. I'm telling you plainly, which is more than most would."

interjections.text: Kessa, approving: "That's the first officer I've liked in nine years."
Aldric: "You could have lied to us." Reed: "Yes."

the_confession.text: Aldric says it in fourteen plain words: a name, a fever, a date and the amount of the draught. Reed writes it down, reads it back, and asks twice if he wants it recorded. Both times he says yes.

interjections.text: Sera, afterwards, in the street: "He just handed a woman with a seal the only thing anyone could hurt him with. On purpose."
Kessa, afterwards: "That took more than a fight would have."

no_law_for_it.text: "Nothing," Reed says. "Rivermark has no law for it, and I won't invent one on a Tuesday. His order has a rule. I have a town." She blots the page. "He can have a copy if he wants. Most people do, eventually."

after_steel.text: "It is," Reed says. "I noticed. Since the quarry, nobody has voted on anything. Things get done, and I've started to enjoy that. I'd like someone to keep an eye on that."

interjections.text: Ilse says nothing and stays by the doorway.

after_pact.text: "Every day, never for more than a minute. There's a goblin factor with a tooth on a wire who comes to the east gate on market day. I have to be seen talking to him. Last month he corrected my arithmetic in front of two carters."

the_watch_roll.text:
Reed looks at the paper in her hand as if someone else had put it there.

"The watch roll," she says. "Twenty-six men, two hundred and ninety gold a quarter, paid in full and on the day for fourteen quarters." She folds it once. "I've fought this council over the price of lamp oil twice in one year."

She lays the folded roll on the well-head between you.

"And I've never once had to fight them over the watch," she says. "It took me fourteen quarters to notice how strange that was. I'd very much like to know what I haven't been fighting about."

interjections.text: Sera, at once: "Then the money isn't coming from the vote. Ask what the vote is."
Kessa: "I've been paid by four people who weren't handing over the money. It's never nothing."

choices.label: I'll find out where the money comes from.
The council found it. That is what a council is for.

payroll_not_the_council.text:
"The council couldn't find eleven gold for the bridge in nine years," says Reed. "I sat through every one of those votes. They're not a body that finds things."

She picks the roll back up.

"Someone is finding this money. Every quarter, on time, without being asked, and without ever wanting public thanks." She looks at you. "I've been a watchman for nineteen years. I've never met anyone who paid for something and didn't want the thanks."

payroll_why_not_her.text:
"Because if the captain of the watch walks into the counting house and asks who's paying her men, the whole town will know by supper," says Reed. "If the answer is dull, I've insulted the council for nothing. If it isn't, I've told whoever it is that I've started looking."

She hands you the folded roll.

"Ashe. Second desk. He won't offer you anything, and he won't refuse you anything either. He's waiting for someone to ask a question. I've been careful for six years not to be the one who asks."

payroll_refused.text:
On quarter day, in front of the council, she sends the money back with her name on the refusal and tells them to find it.

They find about half.

Four men leave the watch within the month: two for the granary, which pays better and always has; one for the stone yard; and one to join a brother at Greyhythe. With nobody to walk it, they drop the west-side night patrol.

"I'll take a smaller watch that's mine," says Captain Elowen Reed, "over a whole one that belongs to someone else." She sounds as if she's said it to herself four hundred times in a fortnight and is still testing the words.

interjections.text: Aldric: "She made the town poorer and herself honest. Both are real, and only one feeds anybody."
Ilse: "She gave back something she needed because she didn't know who it belonged to. There aren't four people in this valley who would."

payroll_kept.text:
Reed is quiet for a while.

"Twenty-six," she says at last, "or eighteen. That's the whole decision. Everything else is how I feel about it."

She writes a note of the arrangement in her own book, in her own hand. She does not put it in the day book, where it would be read.

"There," she says, closing the book. "It's written down, in a drawer. Now I'll have to live with the difference."

interjections.text: Sera: "That's the right answer, and she'll never forgive herself for it. I've seen someone do that before."

payroll_told.text:
She tells them herself in the guardroom. You stand at the back because you wouldn't let her do it alone, and she wouldn't let you do it for her.

It takes four minutes. No one shouts.

They keep the money, every one of them. Six stop calling her Captain when she's out of the room. Ballow, twenty-two years in and at the west gate for the last four, says what the rest of them are thinking:

"Then who is it we work for, serjeant, and how would we know."

interjections.text: Kessa, afterwards: "You've just given twenty-six armed men a thing to think about. I hope you meant to."

choices.label: They had a right to know.

payroll_aftermath.text:
"What I keep coming back to," says Reed, "is that nobody ever asked me for anything."

She turns her cup on the table.

"Not one instruction. Not one favour. For fourteen quarters a stranger paid my men and never once sent word to let a cart through a gate unsearched." She sets the cup down. "So either they haven't needed to ask yet, or I've been doing what they wanted all along without being told. I can't work out which is worse."
